Tyrannosaurus rex. The largest terrestrial predator of the Late Cretaceous period, dominating North American ecosystems approximately 68 to 66 million years ago before the mass extinction event. Standing up to four meters tall and weighing nine metric tons, this bipedal theropod possessed tremendous bite force and sophisticated sensory systems, making it an apex predator of remarkable capability. Fossil evidence reveals that T. rex was likely a skilled hunter with complex behavior, and its lineage represents a direct evolutionary connection to modern birds.

Tyrannosaurus rex lived during the Late Cretaceous period in what is now western North America, in environments of subtropical forests and river valleys.

The massive skull could reach 1.5 meters in length with teeth the size of bananas. The bite force exceeded 12,000 newtons, unmatched by any living animal.

T. rex was bipedal, a two-legged walker, with relatively small but powerful forelimbs bearing sharp claws. The hind legs and tail provided balance and propulsion.

Recent paleontological evidence suggests T. rex was an active hunter capable of moderate speeds of 40 or more kilometers per hour, contrary to the once-popular scavenging hypothesis. Trackways show herding behavior.

The sensory capabilities included excellent vision comparable to modern eagles, sophisticated olfaction, and hearing sensitive to low frequencies for long-distance communication.

Fossil evidence of T. rex specimens shows pathology including healed injuries and infections, suggesting they competed violently with each other and survived dangerous hunts.

The evolutionary lineage from theropods to modern birds is direct. T. rex shares skeletal features with Archaeopteryx and contemporary birds, including a wishbone and hollow bones.

Growth rings in bone fossils indicate T. rex reached sexual maturity around age eighteen to twenty and lived into their late twenties or early thirties before death.

Comparative biomechanical studies show T. rex had the highest bite force of any terrestrial animal ever measured. The feeding strategy emphasized massive crushing force to fragment bone and soft tissue.
